nodes.wikipedia_extract: In computational complexity theory, Håstad's switching lemma is a key tool for proving lower bounds on the size of constant-depth Boolean circuits. It was first introduced by Johan Håstad to prove that AC0 Boolean circuits of depth k require size exp ⁡ ( Ω ( n 1 / ( k − 1 ) ) ) to compute the parity function on n bits. He was later awarded the Gödel Prize for this work in 1994. The switching lemma describes the behavior of a depth-2 circuit under random restriction, i.e. when randomly fixing most of the coordinates to 0 or 1.

nodes.wikipedia_extract: In order theory, the Szpilrajn extension theorem (also called the order-extension principle), proved by Edward Szpilrajn in 1930, states that every partial order is contained in a total order. Intuitively, the theorem says that any method of comparing elements that leaves some pairs incomparable can be extended in such a way that every pair becomes comparable. The theorem is one of many examples of the use of the axiom of choice in the form of Zorn's lemma to find a maximal set with certain properties.

nodes.label: Tait–Kneser theorem
nodes.wikipedia_extract: In differential geometry, the Tait–Kneser theorem states that, if a smooth plane curve has monotonic curvature, then the osculating circles of the curve are disjoint and nested within each other. The logarithmic spiral or the pictured Archimedean spiral provide examples of curves whose curvature is monotonic for the entire curve. This monotonicity cannot happen for a simple closed curve (by the four-vertex theorem, there are at least four vertices where the curvature reaches an extreme point) but for such curves the theorem can be applied to the arcs of the curves between its vertices.

nodes.label: Tameness theorem
nodes.wikipedia_extract: In mathematics, the tameness theorem states that every complete hyperbolic 3-manifold with finitely generated fundamental group is topologically tame, in other words homeomorphic to the interior of a compact 3-manifold. The tameness theorem was conjectured by Marden (1974). It was proved by Agol (2004) and, independently, by Danny Calegari and David Gabai. It is one of the fundamental properties of geometrically infinite hyperbolic 3-manifolds, together with the density theorem for Kleinian groups and the ending lamination theorem. It also implies the Ahlfors measure conjecture.

nodes.wikipedia_extract: In computational complexity theory, the time hierarchy theorems are important statements about time-bounded computation on Turing machines. Informally, these theorems say that given more time, a Turing machine can solve more problems. For example, there are problems that can be solved with n2 time but not n time, where n is the input length. The time hierarchy theorem for deterministic multi-tape Turing machines was first proven by Richard E. Stearns and Juris Hartmanis in 1965. It was improved a year later when F. C. Hennie and Richard E. Stearns improved the efficiency of the universal Turing machine.

More precisely, the Tonelli–Hobson test states that if ƒ is a real-valued measurable function on R2, and either of the two iterated integrals ∫ R ( ∫ R | f ( x , y ) | d x ) d y {\displaystyle \int _{\mathbb {R} }\left(\int _{\mathbb {R} }|f(x,y)|\,dx\right)\,dy} or ∫ R ( ∫ R | f ( x , y ) | d y ) d x {\displaystyle \int _{\mathbb {R} }\left(\int _{\mathbb {R} }|f(x,y)|\,dy\right)\,dx} is finite, then ƒ is Lebesgue-integrable on R2.

nodes.label: Trakhtenbrot's theorem
nodes.wikipedia_extract: In logic, finite model theory, and computability theory, Trakhtenbrot's theorem (due to Boris Trakhtenbrot) states that the problem of validity in first-order logic on the class of all finite models is undecidable. In fact, the class of valid sentences over finite models is not recursively enumerable (though it is co-recursively enumerable). Trakhtenbrot's theorem implies that Gödel's completeness theorem (that is fundamental to first-order logic) does not hold in the finite case. Also it seems counter-intuitive that being valid over all structures is 'easier' than over just the finite ones.

nodes.label: Trudinger's theorem
nodes.wikipedia_extract: In mathematical analysis, Trudinger's theorem or the Trudinger inequality (also sometimes called the Moser–Trudinger inequality) is a result of functional analysis on Sobolev spaces. It is named after Neil Trudinger (and Jürgen Moser). It provides an inequality between a certain Sobolev space norm and an Orlicz space norm of a function. The inequality is a limiting case of Sobolev embedding and can be stated as the following theorem: Let Ω be a bounded domain in R n satisfying the cone condition. Let m p = n and p > 1 . This result is used to calculate the étale cohomology groups of an algebraic curve. The theorem was published by Chiungtze C. Tsen in 1933.

The theorem states that the torque of a resultant of two concurrent forces about any point is equal to the algebraic sum of the torques of its components about the same point. nodes.label: Vaught conjecture
nodes.wikipedia_extract: The Vaught conjecture is a conjecture in the mathematical field of model theory originally proposed by Robert Lawson Vaught in 1961. It states that the number of countable models of a first-order complete theory in a countable language is finite or ℵ0 or 2ℵ0. Morley showed that the number of countable models is finite or ℵ0 or ℵ1 or 2ℵ0, which solves the conjecture except for the case of ℵ1 models when the continuum hypothesis fails. For this remaining case, Robin Knight (2002, 2007) has announced a counterexample to the Vaught conjecture and the topological Vaught conjecture. As of 2021, the counterexample has not been verified.

nodes.label: Veblen's theorem
nodes.wikipedia_extract: In mathematics, Veblen's theorem, introduced by Oswald Veblen (1912), states that the set of edges of a finite graph can be written as a union of disjoint simple cycles if and only if every vertex has even degree. Thus, it is closely related to the theorem of Euler (1736) that a finite graph has an Euler tour (a single non-simple cycle that covers the edges of the graph) if and only if it is connected and every vertex has even degree. Indeed, a representation of a graph as a union of simple cycles may be obtained from an Euler tour by repeatedly splitting the tour into smaller cycles whenever there is a repeated vertex.

nodes.wikipedia_extract: In geometry, the Wallace–Bolyai–Gerwien theorem, named after William Wallace, Farkas Bolyai and P. Gerwien, is a theorem related to dissections of polygons. It answers the question of whether one polygon can be formed from another by cutting it into a finite number of pieces and recomposing these by translations and rotations. The Wallace–Bolyai–Gerwien theorem states that this can be done if and only if two polygons have the same area. Wallace had proven the same result already in 1807. According to other sources, Bolyai and Gerwien had independently proved the theorem in 1833 and 1835, respectively.

nodes.label: Weinstein conjecture
nodes.wikipedia_extract: In mathematics, the Weinstein conjecture refers to a general existence problem for periodic orbits of Hamiltonian or Reeb vector flows. More specifically, the conjecture claims that on a compact contact manifold, its Reeb vector field should carry at least one periodic orbit. By definition, a level set of contact type admits a contact form obtained by contracting the Hamiltonian vector field into the symplectic form. In this case, the Hamiltonian flow is a Reeb vector field on that level set.

nodes.label: Weyl–von Neumann theorem
nodes.wikipedia_extract: In mathematics, the Weyl–von Neumann theorem is a result in operator theory due to Hermann Weyl and John von Neumann. It states that, after the addition of a compact operator (Weyl (1909)) or Hilbert–Schmidt operator (von Neumann (1935)) of arbitrarily small norm, a bounded self-adjoint operator or unitary operator on a Hilbert space is conjugate by a unitary operator to a diagonal operator. The results are subsumed in later generalizations for bounded normal operators due to David Berg (1971, compact perturbation) and Dan-Virgil Voiculescu (1979, Hilbert–Schmidt perturbation).

This is the best linear bound on the smallest-dimensional Euclidean space that all m-dimensional manifolds embed in, as the real projective spaces of dimension m cannot be embedded into real (2m − 1)-space if m is a power of two (as can be seen from a characteristic class argument, also due to Whitney).

nodes.wikipedia_extract: In mathematical analysis, Wiener's Tauberian theorem is any of several related results proved by Norbert Wiener in 1932. Informally, if the Fourier transform of a function f vanishes on a certain set Z , the Fourier transform of any linear combination of translations of f also vanishes on Z .

nodes.wikipedia_extract: The Wigner–Eckart theorem is a theorem of representation theory and quantum mechanics. It states that matrix elements of spherical tensor operators in the basis of angular momentum eigenstates can be expressed as the product of two factors, one of which is independent of angular momentum orientation, and the other a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient. The name derives from physicists Eugene Wigner and Carl Eckart, who developed the formalism as a link between the symmetry transformation groups of space (applied to the Schrödinger equations) and the principles of conservation of energy, momentum, and angular momentum.

edges.note: The argument principle is proved by showing that each zero of order k of f gives a simple pole of f'/f with residue k and each pole of order m gives residue -m, and then applying the residue theorem to the contour integral of f'/f.

In the proof of the Wedderburn–Artin theorem the ring is written as a product of matrix rings over the endomorphism rings of its simple right ideals, and these endomorphism rings are division rings by Schur's lemma.

Wikipedia's proof of Arzelà–Ascoli enumerates the rational points of the interval, uses Bolzano–Weierstrass at each one to pass to a subsequence converging there, and takes the diagonal subsequence, which converges at every rational point.

A common proof of the Banach–Alaoglu theorem identifies the dual unit ball, in the weak-* topology, with a closed subset of a product of compact sets; the product is compact by Tychonoff's theorem, hence so is the ball.

The proof of the Banach–Tarski paradox uses the axiom of choice to pick one point from every orbit of a free group of rotations acting on the sphere; the axiom of choice is what allows the non-measurable pieces to be constructed.

edges.note: The proof of the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem uses Hall's marriage theorem to find a permutation matrix supported on the nonzero entries of a doubly stochastic matrix, then removes scalar multiples of permutation matrices one after another until the zero matrix is reached.

The least-upper-bound property, one form of the completeness axiom of the real numbers, can be used to prove the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem: the page's proof takes the least upper bound of the set of points that lie below infinitely many terms of the sequence.

edges.note: The proof drops perpendiculars from the point to the four sides and applies the Pythagorean theorem to the resulting right triangles to express each squared corner distance.

The proof of Burnside's lemma rewrites the sum of fixed-point counts as a sum of stabilizer orders over points, then uses the orbit–stabilizer theorem (with Lagrange's theorem) to replace each stabilizer order by |G| divided by the orbit size, which counts orbits.

edges.note: The proof of Cauchy's mean value theorem defines h(x) = (g(b)-g(a))f(x) - (f(b)-f(a))g(x), checks h(a) = h(b), and applies Rolle's theorem to h to get a point c with h'(c) = 0.

Many texts prove Cauchy's theorem by strong induction with the class equation: if p does not divide the order of the center, some non-central conjugacy class has size not divisible by p, so p divides the order of a proper centralizer and induction applies.

Cauchy's theorem is a partial converse to Lagrange's theorem: Lagrange says subgroup orders divide the group order, and Cauchy gives a subgroup of order p for every prime p dividing the group order. The page's inductive proof argues with subgroup orders and indices [G:H].

edges.note: The characteristic-function proof of the central limit theorem shows that the characteristic functions of the normalized sums converge to that of the standard normal, and Lévy's continuity theorem turns this into convergence in distribution.
Chebyshev's inequality follows by applying Markov's inequality to the non-negative random variable (X − μ)².
The generic Chernoff bound is obtained by applying Markov's inequality to e^(tX), giving a tail bound in terms of the moment-generating function, and then taking the infimum over t.

The constructive existence proofs use Bézout's identity for the coprime moduli (m1·n1 + m2·n2 = 1 for two moduli, M_i·N_i + m_i·n_i = 1 in the direct construction) to write down the solution, and the page says its proofs are based on Euclid's lemma and Bézout's identity.

The size of a conjugacy class equals the index of the centralizer, which is the orbit–stabilizer theorem for the conjugation action (classes are orbits, centralizers are stabilizers); summing over classes gives the class equation.

In the proof of the Cramér–Rao bound, the covariance of the estimator T with the score V equals the derivative of the estimator's expectation, and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds that covariance by the square root of var(T) times var(V), where var(V) is the Fisher information.

edges.note: A proof of the de Moivre–Laplace theorem replaces the factorials in the binomial coefficient by Stirling's formula and simplifies to the Gaussian expression.

Dirichlet's approximation theorem is proved by the pigeonhole principle: the fractional parts of kα for k = 0, ..., N are N+1 numbers in [0,1), which is cut into N intervals of length 1/N, so two of them fall in the same interval.

Conrad's proof of Dirichlet's unit theorem uses Minkowski's convex-body theorem, which he calls a standard tool for proofs of the unit theorem; Dirichlet's own 1846 proof used the pigeonhole principle instead.

Wikipedia's proof of the divergence theorem reduces to integrating one partial derivative along its own coordinate and evaluates that inner integral by the fundamental theorem of calculus; in one dimension the divergence theorem reduces to the fundamental theorem of calculus.
The direct proof of the dominated convergence theorem uses Fatou's lemma as its essential tool: the reverse Fatou lemma is applied to |f - f_n|, which is bounded above by the integrable function 2g.

Donsker's theorem is a functional extension of the central limit theorem: the CLT gives convergence at a fixed point (or finitely many points, via the multinomial central limit approximation), and Donsker's theorem extends the convergence to the whole random function.

edges.note: Label each term of the sequence with the lengths of the longest increasing and longest decreasing subsequences ending there. The labels are all different, so by the pigeonhole principle one label must fall outside the (r-1)(s-1) allowed pairs, which gives a long monotone subsequence.
A common modern proof: if n divides ab and a, n are coprime, Bézout's identity gives rn + sa = 1; multiplying by b gives rnb + sab = b, and both terms on the left are divisible by n, so n divides b.

In the proof of the Euler product formula for the zeta function, the fundamental theorem of arithmetic is what makes the expanded partial product over primes equal the sum of the terms n^(−s) over the integers n built from those primes.

The page's main proof starts from Fermat's little theorem, a^(p-1) = 1 mod p, factors it as (a^((p-1)/2) - 1)(a^((p-1)/2) + 1) = 0 mod p, and shows residues make the first factor zero and nonresidues the second.

edges.target: Central Force Motion and the Kepler Problem

edges.note: Wikipedia's proof of the extreme value theorem takes a sequence in [a,b] along which f is unbounded, or along which f approaches its supremum, and uses Bolzano–Weierstrass to extract a convergent subsequence; continuity at the limit then gives boundedness and attainment of the supremum.

The proof of Fermat's Last Theorem rests on the modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves, proved by Wiles and Taylor: a solution of Fermat's equation would give a semistable elliptic curve that cannot be modular.

Ribet's theorem (the epsilon conjecture) shows that a solution of Fermat's equation for a prime exponent would give a semistable elliptic curve that cannot be modular; together with modularity of semistable curves this implies Fermat's Last Theorem.

The proof of the five color theorem uses the Euler characteristic of the plane (V − E + F = 2 for a connected plane graph) to show that a simple planar graph has a vertex of degree at most five, which is the vertex removed in the induction.

The proof of the Fourier inversion theorem inserts a Gaussian factor exp(-pi eps^2 |xi|^2) into the inversion integral, uses the dominated convergence theorem (the transform is assumed integrable) to pass to the limit eps -> 0, and then uses Fubini's theorem and an approximation to the identity.

Frobenius' theorem generalizes the existence theorem for ordinary differential equations: a single vector field always has integral curves (their existence is guaranteed by the Picard–Lindelöf theorem), and Frobenius gives the compatibility conditions under which the integral curves of r vector fields mesh into r-dimensional integral manifolds.

In the standard proof, monotone convergence extends the iterated-integral identity from simple functions to non-negative measurable functions, which is Tonelli's theorem; Fubini's theorem for integrable functions then follows by applying Tonelli's theorem to the positive and negative parts.

Wikipedia's proof of the second part of the fundamental theorem of calculus applies the mean value theorem on each subinterval of a partition to turn F(b) - F(a) into a Riemann sum of F'; the corollary form also uses the mean value theorem to show that two antiderivatives differ by a constant.

The uniqueness half of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic is proved with Euclid's lemma: a prime in one factorization divides the product in the other, so by Euclid's lemma it divides, and hence equals, one of its primes.

The proof writes the Frenet–Serret formulas as a first-order linear ODE system for the frame and applies Picard's existence-and-uniqueness theorem to get the frame from given curvature and torsion, then integrates the tangent vector to get the curve. Uniqueness of ODE solutions is also used to show the frame stays orthonormal.

edges.note: The proof of Gauss's lemma evaluates a product of least residues in two ways to get a^((p-1)/2) = (-1)^n modulo p, and Euler's criterion identifies a^((p-1)/2) with the Legendre symbol (a/p).

In the proof of the local Gauss-Bonnet theorem, the geodesic curvature integrated along the boundary of a patch splits into a turning-angle term and the line integral of a 1-form X with dX = K dV; Green's theorem converts that line integral into the integral of the Gaussian curvature over the patch.
The proof of the Gauss–Lucas theorem begins by using the fundamental theorem of algebra to write the polynomial as a product of linear factors over its complex zeros.

edges.note: For each fixed x the empirical distribution function converges almost surely to F(x) by the strong law of large numbers; the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem strengthens this to uniform convergence, and its proof applies the strong law at finitely many points.

Green's theorem extends the fundamental theorem of calculus to two dimensions, and its proof (OpenStax, for a rectangle) evaluates the inner integral of each partial derivative by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

The proof of the Green–Tao theorem is an extension of Szemerédi's theorem: Szemerédi's theorem does not apply directly to the primes because they have density zero, so a transference principle (a relative Szemerédi theorem) extends it to subsets of pseudorandom sets.

The proof of the first incompleteness theorem needs a sentence that indirectly asserts its own unprovability; the existence of such a sentence follows from the diagonal lemma (Gödel himself constructed the sentence directly).

The proof of the first incompleteness theorem needs a sentence that indirectly asserts its own unprovability; the existence of such a sentence follows from the diagonal lemma (Gödel himself constructed the sentence directly).

The second incompleteness theorem is an extension of the first: once the facts about provability used in the first theorem's proof are formalized inside the system, the second theorem follows by formalizing the entire proof of the first theorem within the system.

In the proof of the Hadamard factorization theorem, Jensen's formula bounds the number n(r) of zeros in a disc by the growth of the function (n(r) log 2 <= log M(2r)), which shows that the exponent of convergence of the zeros is at most the order.

The standard proof of the general Hahn–Banach theorem extends the functional one dimension at a time (a one-dimensional extension lemma) and uses Zorn's lemma to obtain an extension to the whole space; the strictly weaker ultrafilter lemma can be used instead.

The ham sandwich theorem is proved by a reduction to the Borsuk–Ulam theorem: a continuous function on the sphere of directions records how each bisecting hyperplane splits the other objects, and Borsuk–Ulam gives antipodal points with equal values, which is the simultaneous bisection.

A common proof of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality uses the Vitali covering lemma to select disjoint balls whose fivefold enlargements cover the set where the maximal function is large, which gives the weak-type (1,1) estimate.

The least-upper-bound property can be used to prove the Heine–Borel theorem for a closed interval [a, b]: take the least upper bound of the set of points s such that [a, s] is covered by finitely many of the open sets, and show that it equals b.

Hoeffding's inequality is proved by the Chernoff method (Markov's inequality applied to the exponential of the sum of independent variables), with Hoeffding's lemma bounding the moment generating functions of the bounded variables.
The proof of Hölder's inequality normalizes f and g and applies Young's inequality for products, ab ≤ a^p/p + b^q/q, pointwise before integrating.

The identity theorem is established from the fact that a holomorphic function can be expanded into its Taylor series (analyticity of holomorphic functions); the proof compares the Taylor expansions of the two functions.
Integration by parts is derived by integrating the product rule; the definite-integral form then follows by applying the fundamental theorem of calculus to the difference between the two endpoints.

The standard proof of the intermediate value theorem takes the set of points where f stays below the target value; the least upper bound property supplies the supremum of that set, and continuity forces f to equal the target there.

The intersecting chords theorem is proved by triangle similarity: the inscribed angle theorem gives equal angles on a common chord, so the two triangles at the crossing point are similar and their side ratios give the product rule.
The proof of invariance of domain uses tools of algebraic topology, notably the Brouwer fixed-point theorem.
The textbook proof of the inverse function theorem obtains the local inverse as the fixed point of a contraction, using the contraction mapping principle (Banach fixed-point theorem).

Brouwer's theorem is a special case of Kakutani's, and Kakutani's theorem is deduced from it: the approximate selection theorem gives continuous maps whose graphs approach the graph of the set-valued map, Brouwer's theorem gives each a fixed point, and a convergent subsequence gives a fixed point of the set-valued map.

edges.note: In the proof of the Kolmogorov extension theorem the consistent finite-dimensional measures define a countably additive set function on the semiring of cylinder sets, and the Carathéodory extension theorem extends it to a unique measure on the product σ-algebra.

The proof of the Krein–Milman theorem uses the Hahn–Banach separation theorem: if a point of K lay outside the closed convex hull of the extreme points, a continuous linear functional would separate it from that hull, and the set where the functional is maximal on K leads to a contradiction.

Kőnig's theorem is stated under the axiom of choice (without it the sum and product cannot be defined as cardinal numbers), and its proof uses choice to show the product is non-empty and to pick, for each index, an element outside the image of the corresponding summand.

Wikipedia's general proof of L'Hôpital's rule uses Cauchy's mean value theorem to write the ratio (f(x) - f(y)) / (g(x) - g(y)) as f'(ξ)/g'(ξ) at an intermediate point, and the ordinary mean value theorem to show g(x) - g(y) is nonzero.

edges.note: The law of cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem, and its usual proof (Euclid's) drops a perpendicular and applies the Pythagorean theorem to the two right triangles formed.
Under the assumption of finite variance, the weak law of large numbers is proved by noting that the sample mean has variance σ²/n and applying Chebyshev's inequality to it.

For simple random walk, the law of the iterated logarithm is proved with the Borel–Cantelli lemma along the geometric sequence a^k: summable tail estimates give the upper bound (first lemma), and non-summable probabilities of increment events give the lower bound (second lemma).

In the Lax-Richtmyer proof, the direction 'a convergent scheme is necessarily stable' shows the scheme's operators are bounded on each initial element and then appeals to the principle of uniform boundedness to conclude they are uniformly bounded, which is the definition of stability; the direction 'stable implies convergent' does not need it.

In the proof, the Riesz representation theorem turns the continuous linear form L into a vector f and the continuous bilinear form a into a bounded operator A with a(u,v) = ⟨Au,v⟩, so the problem becomes Au = f; coercivity then shows that A is a bijection.

The Lebesgue differentiation theorem, in the strong form that almost every point is a Lebesgue point, is proved in the standard treatment from the weak-L^1 estimate for the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function.
The standard proof of the Lebesgue differentiation theorem rests on the weak-type estimate for the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function, and the Vitali covering lemma is what proves that estimate.

The proof sketch first applies the simplicial approximation theorem: if the map has no fixed points it is homotopic, after subdividing, to a fixed-point-free simplicial map, whose induced maps on the simplicial chain complex have zero diagonal entries and hence zero traces, so the Lefschetz number is zero.
The integral formula bounds f'(z) by sup|f|/R, which tends to zero for a bounded entire function.

The proof of Löb's theorem applies a fixed point of the formula X → P, a sentence Ψ equivalent to (□Ψ → P); when □ is provability in Peano arithmetic, the existence of such fixed points follows from the diagonal lemma.

The upward part of the Löwenheim–Skolem theorem is proved by adding κ many new constant symbols, with sentences saying they are pairwise distinct, to the elementary diagram of the model and applying the compactness theorem to see that the resulting theory is consistent.

The maximum modulus principle is proved from Cauchy's integral formula: either directly, or through Gauss's mean value theorem (a consequence of the formula), which forces the function to be constant on overlapping disks once the modulus has an interior maximum.

Wikipedia's proof of the mean value theorem subtracts a linear function rx from f, with r chosen so the new function takes equal values at the endpoints, and applies Rolle's theorem to it. Rolle's theorem is the special case f(a) = f(b).
The standard proof of the Minkowski inequality writes |f+g|^p as |f+g| times |f+g|^(p-1), applies the triangle inequality, and then applies Hölder's inequality to each of the two resulting integrals.

In the standard proof of Montel's theorem, Cauchy's integral formula shows that a locally bounded family of holomorphic functions is locally uniformly equicontinuous, and the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem then gives that the family is normal.

The proof of Morera's theorem constructs an antiderivative F of f, which is holomorphic, and then uses that holomorphic functions are analytic to conclude that f = F' is holomorphic. That analyticity fact is itself proved from Cauchy's integral formula.

edges.note: In the commutative case Nakayama's lemma is a simple consequence of a generalized form of the Cayley–Hamilton theorem: a standard proof uses the determinant trick, a Cayley–Hamilton-type identity for an endomorphism of a finitely generated module.
Rouché's theorem shows every value near f(z₀) is attained, so images of disks contain disks.

The standard proof of the open mapping theorem for Banach spaces uses the Baire category theorem to show that the closure of the image of a ball contains a ball (the map is nearly open); completeness of the domain then upgrades nearly open to open.

edges.note: The orbit–stabilizer theorem gives a bijection between the orbit of x and the cosets of its stabilizer; for a finite group, combining it with Lagrange's theorem gives |orbit| = |G| / |stabilizer|.

edges.note: The proof on the page approximates f by Lipschitz functions, forms Picard iterations, shows they are equicontinuous, and uses the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem to extract uniformly convergent subsequences whose limit solves the equation.

The Phragmen-Lindeloef principle generalizes the maximum modulus principle to unbounded domains, and its proof multiplies f by an auxiliary factor that tames its growth and then applies the maximum modulus principle on a bounded subregion.

A standard proof turns the differential equation into an integral equation; the integral (Picard) operator is a contraction, so the Banach fixed-point theorem gives existence and uniqueness of the solution.

edges.note: In the proof, a solution arc between two crossings of a transverse curve, together with the piece of that curve between the crossings, forms a closed curve. The Jordan curve theorem says it divides the plane into two regions and the solution then stays in one of them, which makes successive crossings monotone.

Newman's short proof of the prime number theorem relies on complex analysis, using Cauchy's integral formula, Cauchy's integral theorem and estimates of complex integrals; Cauchy's integral theorem is used to deform part of the contour without changing the integral.
The proof by similar triangles starts from equal inscribed angles on the same chord of the circumcircle; these give the two pairs of similar triangles whose side ratios add up to Ptolemy's relation.

The Pólya enumeration theorem follows from Burnside's lemma: the unweighted form is Burnside's orbit count applied to colorings, and the weighted form applies Burnside's lemma separately to the orbits of each weight.
Proofs of quadratic reciprocity on the fetched page (Eisenstein's lemma, Gauss sums) use Euler's criterion to identify a^((p-1)/2) mod p with the Legendre symbol (a/p).

edges.target: Dark Energy and the Cosmological Constant

edges.note: The page's proofs of Ramsey-type bounds use the pigeonhole principle on the edges at a vertex: for example, of the 5 edges at a vertex of a 2-coloured K6 at least 3 have the same colour, which gives R(3,3) ≤ 6.

In the proof of the Rellich-Kondrachov theorem, the mollified functions of a bounded family are equibounded and equicontinuous, so the Arzela-Ascoli theorem makes them relatively compact in C^0; this compactness is then transferred to L^q because mollification changes the functions by a uniformly small amount.

The standard proof of the residue theorem uses Cauchy's integral theorem (Cauchy–Goursat): the function is holomorphic away from the singularities, so the contour integral reduces to a sum of integrals around small loops enclosing each singularity. The residue theorem in turn generalizes Cauchy's integral theorem.

Rice's theorem is proved by reduction from the halting problem: an algorithm deciding any non-trivial semantic property would give an algorithm deciding halting, which is impossible. The theorem generalizes the undecidability of the halting problem.

In the normal-families proof of the Riemann mapping theorem, the family of univalent maps of the domain into the unit disk is normal by Montel's theorem, so a sequence maximizing f'(a) has a subsequence converging uniformly on compacta to the extremal map.

For continuous compactly supported f, the Fourier transform is bounded by half the integral of |f(x) - f(x + pi/xi)|, which tends to 0 by the dominated convergence theorem; a general integrable f is then approximated in L^1 by such functions.

In the existence proof of the Hilbert-space Riesz theorem the kernel K of the functional is closed, so H = K ⊕ K^⊥; the page defers the proof of this decomposition to the Hilbert projection theorem, and the representing vector is built from a non-zero p in K^⊥.

In the form 'L^p is complete', the Riesz-Fischer theorem is proved from the convergence theorems for the Lebesgue integral: for a series with summable L^p norms, the Minkowski inequality and the monotone convergence theorem show the sum of absolute values is finite almost everywhere and lies in L^p; dominated convergence then gives convergence in norm.

The proof of Rolle's theorem finds an interior maximum or minimum and shows the derivative is zero there, which is exactly the statement of Fermat's theorem on stationary points; Wikipedia notes that Fermat's theorem can be applied directly for that step.

Rouché's theorem is proved with the argument principle: under the hypothesis the image curves of the two functions wind around the origin the same number of times (the winding number is homotopy-invariant), and the argument principle turns equal winding numbers into equal numbers of zeros.

The proof of Sard's theorem is by induction on the dimension of the domain: after a change of coordinates each slice of the set of critical values is null by the inductive hypothesis, and Tonelli's theorem (a variant of Fubini's theorem) then shows the whole set is null.

Schauder's theorem extends Brouwer's theorem to infinite-dimensional spaces, and its proof maps the compact convex set into the convex hull of finitely many points, applies the Brouwer fixed-point theorem there to get approximate fixed points, and passes to a limit by compactness.
The Schreier refinement theorem is often proved using the Zassenhaus (butterfly) lemma.
The Schwarz lemma is proved by applying the maximum modulus principle to g(z) = f(z)/z on the closed disks of radius r < 1 and letting r tend to 1, which gives |g| <= 1.

The Schwarz reflection principle is proved from Morera's theorem: a contour integral of the reflected extension splits into two pieces along the real axis, each of which vanishes, so the extension is holomorphic across the axis.

edges.note: The existence proof of the SVD headed 'Based on the spectral theorem' applies the spectral theorem to the Hermitian positive semi-definite matrix M*M to obtain the unitary matrix V of its eigenvectors.
Slutsky's theorem follows from joint convergence in distribution of (X_n, Y_n) to (X, c) and then the continuous mapping theorem applied to the continuous functions x + y, xy and x/y.

The Sobolev embedding follows from the Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev inequality, whose proof bounds |u| by one-dimensional integrals of |Du| along each coordinate line, multiplies these bounds, and integrates one variable at a time using the generalized Hoelder inequality; the case 1 < p < n applies Hoelder's inequality once more.

edges.note: Stewart's theorem is proved by applying the law of cosines in the two small triangles on either side of the cevian, whose angles at the cevian's foot are supplementary, and eliminating the cosine.

edges.note: The page's proof of the strong law (i.i.d. variables with finite fourth moment) bounds the probabilities of the deviation events so that they are summable, and the Borel–Cantelli lemma then gives almost-sure convergence.

Tarski's undefinability theorem is proved by contradiction: if a truth formula existed, the diagonal lemma applied to its negation would give a 'liar' sentence equivalent to its own untruth; the general form of the theorem is stated for any language in which the diagonal lemma holds.

The mean-value forms of the remainder in Taylor's theorem (Lagrange and Cauchy forms) are proved with the mean value theorem, in Wikipedia's proof through Cauchy's mean value theorem, and the case k = 0 of the theorem is the mean value theorem itself.

edges.note: The transversality theorem says that transversality is a generic property of smooth maps. That genericity is proved from Sard's theorem, which says the critical values of a smooth map form a set of measure zero.
The proof of the Tietze extension theorem builds the extension as a limit of approximations, and each approximating function comes from Urysohn's lemma applied to two disjoint closed sets.
Titu's lemma (Sedrakyan's inequality, Engel's form) is a direct consequence of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

Tonelli's theorem is proved by checking the iterated-integral identity for indicator and simple functions and then extending it to all non-negative measurable functions with the monotone convergence theorem, since every such function is an increasing limit of simple functions.

edges.note: The standard short proof of the uniform boundedness principle writes the Banach space as the union of the closed sets X_n where the family is bounded by n; by the Baire category theorem one X_n has non-empty interior, which gives a uniform bound.

In the proof of the Urysohn metrization theorem, Urysohn's lemma supplies countably many continuous functions to [0,1], one for each suitable pair of basic open sets, and together they embed the space in the Hilbert cube, which is metrizable.
Łoś's theorem is proved by induction on the complexity of the formula, and the axiom of choice is needed at the existential quantifier step.
