principles.statement: In a curved space, straight paths that start out side by side drift together or apart at a rate set by the curvature. If the curvature is known only to lie above or below some value, the paths can be compared with those in a simple model space of exactly that curvature. This turns a local bound into global conclusions, such as a space having finite size or paths being forced to end.
principles.title: A bound on curvature controls how fast neighbouring straight paths come together

principles.statement: If the cost of a choice curves upward like a bowl, and the allowed choices form a region without dents, any choice that small changes cannot improve is already the best overall. Searching downhill cannot get stuck in a false dip, and a matching companion problem can often certify that nothing better exists. Many fitting methods are designed to have this shape for that reason.
principles.title: A bowl-shaped problem has no false dips so local improvement finds the best answer

principles.statement: Smooth laws of change can be imitated by many small steps, each using only nearby information. Simulations on grids of cells and even layered neural networks can be read as such step-by-step versions of a continuous process.
principles.title: A continuous law can be replaced by many small local steps

principles.statement: A set of statements picks out the things that satisfy it, and a collection of things picks out the statements true of all of them. These two directions fit together exactly, so one side can be studied through the other, and simplified descriptions can still give safe answers about the real things.
principles.title: A description and the things that satisfy it determine each other

principles.statement: Once interactions are included, waves and oscillators stop adding simply. A handful of equations capture the main effects, such as waves that hold their shape and oscillators that fall into step, and they recur in condensed matter, optics, electronics and biology.
principles.title: A few nonlinear equations describe waves and oscillations everywhere

principles.statement: If no point anywhere in space acts as a source or a sink of a field, the field can be written as the swirl of another field. That hidden field is not unique: many choices give the same visible field, and picking one is a matter of convenience. In the same way a field with no swirl anywhere can be written as the slope of a single quantity. If the region has holes these hidden fields may fail to exist.
principles.title: A field with no sources anywhere can be produced from a hidden potential field

principles.statement: Instead of inventing a method for every new problem, one can translate the problem into a form for which a good method already exists. If the translation is faithful and does not make the problem much larger, an answer found there translates back into an answer to the original. Planning tasks rewritten as logic formulas for a general-purpose solver work this way. So do field problems on an awkward region, carried to a disc or half-plane by a change of shape that leaves the governing equation unchanged.
principles.title: A hard problem can be solved by translating it into one that is already solved

principles.statement: If the world has more dimensions than we see, an observer confined to a slice of it only sees their shadow. Small or hidden directions show up as extra fields, towers of masses, or extra terms in the slice's own equations. Working out what the slice inherits from the larger space is a geometry problem.
principles.title: A higher-dimensional world looks like extra fields and masses from inside a lower-dimensional slice

principles.statement: If a region has no dents, so that the straight segment between any two of its points stays inside it, and it includes its own edge, then any point outside can be separated from it by a single flat boundary. That boundary is a simple linear test which the outside point fails and every member of the region passes. Such a test certifies that the point lies outside even when checking membership directly is hard.
principles.title: A point outside a region without dents can be cut off from it by one flat wall

principles.statement: If every step of a procedure makes some quantity strictly larger, and that quantity cannot keep increasing without end, the procedure must finish after finitely many steps. The same holds for a quantity that strictly shrinks and cannot shrink forever. Showing that such a chain has to level off is a common way to prove that a search or completion procedure terminates, even when no bound on its running time is known.
principles.title: A process that keeps enlarging something that cannot grow forever must stop

principles.statement: A proof that one statement follows from another can be read as a program that turns evidence for the first into evidence for the second, and types play the role of statements. The mathematics that describes functions and their composition describes both, which is why proof assistants are also programming languages.
principles.title: A proof and a program are the same object seen two ways

principles.statement: Some properties can be confirmed after seeing only a finite amount, such as a program having printed a given line, even though not seeing it yet proves nothing. Such properties combine the way open regions of a space do: any number joined with or, and finitely many joined with and, are still confirmable. Treating them this way lets ideas of nearness and continuity describe what a computation can observe.
principles.title: A property that finite evidence can confirm behaves like an open region

principles.statement: If a quantity at each point keeps moving toward the average of the values around it, bumps flatten out and no new highest or lowest point can form inside a region. Once it has settled, each value equals the average of its neighbours, so the extremes can only sit at the edges. Temperature in a solid and the electric potential in empty space behave this way, which is also why a charged particle cannot be held in stable balance by static electric forces alone.
principles.title: A quantity pulled toward the average of its surroundings smooths out and makes no new peaks

principles.statement: When a result is built from many independent random inputs and no single input can change it much, the result stays very close to its average. This is why an average over a large sample can be trusted. It is also the starting point for showing that a model's error on enough examples is a fair guide to its error on new ones, although a model fitted to those same examples needs extra care.
principles.title: A quantity that depends a little on each of many independent things barely varies

principles.statement: Any number computed from random trials, such as an average score, would come out somewhat differently if the trials were repeated. How much it would vary can be estimated from the trials themselves. A claim that one method beats another is only as reliable as that estimate of spread.
principles.title: A result measured from a few random trials is itself uncertain

principles.statement: Some problems are easiest to solve crudely first. A rule that turns an approximate answer into a better one can then be repeated, and from a good enough start each round gains accuracy. Finding roots of equations works this way both for ordinary numbers and for remainders modulo higher and higher powers of a prime.
principles.title: A rough answer can be sharpened step by step until it is as accurate as needed

principles.statement: Many sequences, from daily measurements to sentences, can be described by a rule that predicts each new entry from the entries before it. Multiplying those one-step predictions gives the probability of the whole sequence, and running the rule forward produces new sequences. The rule can be as simple as a weighted sum of recent values or as elaborate as a large network; these share the step-by-step form but are not the same model.
principles.title: A sequence can be generated one step at a time from what came before

principles.statement: Many calculations produce an answer as a sum of ever smaller corrections. Sometimes the corrections shrink at first and later grow, so the whole sum has no value, yet stopping near the smallest correction gives an excellent approximation. Telling whether and where a series settles is then part of the calculation.
principles.title: A series that never settles can still give excellent answers if cut off in time

principles.statement: When many particles or light rays move smoothly but begin to overtake one another, the map from where they started to where they are folds over. Along the fold the density becomes very large, giving sharp bright lines like the curve of light at the bottom of a coffee cup. In typical cases only a few standard shapes of fold can occur, so the same patterns recur in very different settings.
principles.title: A smooth motion that folds over itself piles up along sharp edges

principles.statement: When whatever produces a field is concentrated on a surface instead of spread through a volume, the field does not pass smoothly through that surface. Some part of it, or of its rate of change, differs abruptly from one side to the other, and the size of the difference is set by the amount of source sitting on the surface. Electric charge on a surface and matter on a thin wall in gravity both behave this way.
principles.title: A source squeezed onto a thin sheet shows up as a jump across it

principles.statement: A space can be cut into a stack of lower-dimensional slices. The shape of the whole is then recorded as the shape inside each slice, how each slice bends, and how neighbouring slices fit together. This turns a question about the whole space into a question about slices changing from one to the next.
principles.title: A space can be understood one slice at a time

principles.statement: Many spaces look like ordinary flat space in any small region yet join up differently as a whole, like the surface of the Earth or a ring. Describing such a space by overlapping flat maps separates what can be seen nearby from the shape of the whole. The spacetime of gravity and the spaces of positions of a mechanical system are both treated this way.
principles.title: A space that looks flat up close can still have a different overall shape

principles.statement: Some quantities are found by adding a contribution from every route a system could take. After a mathematical change of the time variable, each route is weighted the way a random walk would weight it, and the sum becomes an ordinary average over randomly wandering paths. In that form the sum has a precise meaning, and the equations of quantum motion are tied to those of heat and diffusion.
principles.title: A sum over every possible history can be turned into an average over random paths

principles.statement: A rule may treat several possibilities exactly alike while the state it settles into favours one of them. The symmetry is then not gone: it turns the several equally good settled states into one another. Which symmetries a settled state still keeps, and which it has lost, can be counted. That count predicts what is observed, such as how many new kinds of ripple appear or how many carriers of a force become heavy.
principles.title: A symmetric law can settle into a state that is not symmetric

principles.statement: A system that watches a signal of how it is doing and adjusts its input in response can hold itself near a target without knowing the disturbances in advance. Senders that slow down when they see delay or loss are one example. Whether the loop settles or oscillates depends on how strongly and how quickly it reacts.
principles.title: A system can steer itself by measuring its own output and correcting

principles.statement: When a system is too complicated to describe in detail, its inner workings can be replaced by a random pick from all possibilities that respect its symmetries. Statistical features computed this way, such as the spacing between energy levels, often match experiment and come out the same for many different systems. For those features the class of symmetry matters and the details do not.
principles.title: A system too tangled to follow can be modelled by a random one with the same symmetries

principles.statement: For systems that respond in proportion to what is done to them, the reaction to one sharp, concentrated push contains everything. Any other input is a sum of such pushes, and requirements such as effects not coming before causes or waves leaving without returning put strong limits on that basic response.
principles.title: A system's response to a single sharp kick determines its response to everything

principles.statement: A table of records can be read as the list of cases in which some statement holds: each row says the statement is true of those values. A question about the data then becomes a logical statement, and answering it means finding every case that makes the statement true. This lets the rules of logic be used to write, check and simplify questions about stored data.
principles.title: A table of facts lists the cases where a statement is true

principles.statement: Physicists can calculate with a theory and match experiments for decades while nobody has shown that the theory is mathematically well defined. Turning working calculations into a proof that the object exists, with the properties the calculations suggest, is a separate and often much harder problem.
principles.title: A theory can give correct predictions long before anyone proves it is mathematically sound

principles.statement: Some objects are pinned down completely by a modest set of partial views: a number by its remainders, a curve by a few of its values, an image by its shadows from many directions. This makes it possible to split a secret, reconstruct an image, or solve a hard problem in small pieces and lift the answer back up.
principles.title: A whole can be rebuilt from enough of its pieces

principles.statement: Any rule that sorts cases into yes and no makes two kinds of mistake: raising a false alarm and missing a real case. Making the rule stricter cuts one kind of mistake and raises the other. Which balance is right depends on what each mistake costs and on how common real cases are.
principles.title: A yes-or-no test trades missed cases against false alarms

principles.statement: Many real things are smooth almost everywhere but break sharply along a few lines or surfaces: the outline of an object in a photograph, a shock front in a gas, a crack in a solid. A framework that measures the total amount of change, counting each jump by its size, can describe the smooth parts and the breaks together. Problems that ask for the best such description can then be solved without knowing in advance where the breaks are.
principles.title: Allowing sudden jumps lets one description cover both smooth stretches and sharp edges

principles.statement: When there are far too many possibilities to add up, a random walk that visits them in the right proportions gives the average instead. Following one system for a long time can stand in for averaging over all its states. The method only works as well as the walk mixes, and it slows down where the system itself is slow.
principles.title: An average over all possibilities can be estimated by wandering through them at random

principles.statement: If a theory matches what is observed only when its adjustable settings lie in a tiny range, most of its possible settings predict something else. Weighing a theory by how much of its whole range of settings fits the data, and not by its best fit alone, counts that tuning against it. This automatic penalty on contrived explanations is a precise form of preferring simple ones.
principles.title: An explanation that works only with finely tuned settings is less believable

principles.statement: Once there is a reasonable way to say how far apart two things are, whether strings, probability distributions or model settings, ideas from geometry such as shortest paths, curvature and steepest descent can often be used on them. Choosing the right distance often makes a problem easier.
principles.title: Any collection with a sensible distance can be treated as a geometric space

principles.statement: When a medium changes abruptly across a moving front, the mass, momentum and energy flowing into one side must flow out of the other. That bookkeeping alone ties the jump in density to the jumps in pressure and temperature and to the speed of the front. Measuring one jump can therefore tell how fast the front is moving, once the state of the medium ahead of it is known.
principles.title: Balancing what crosses a sudden front fixes how its two sides differ

principles.statement: A small change in a setting can change a system's overall behavior in kind once the setting passes a critical value: a network suddenly connects, a magnet picks a direction, a steady flow becomes unstable, a puzzle goes from almost always solvable to almost always unsolvable. In systems made of many random parts the change is gradual at small sizes and becomes sharp, happening at a single point, only in the limit of a very large system. In a system that follows a fixed rule of motion the change can be sharp at any size.
principles.title: Behavior changes abruptly when a parameter crosses a sharp threshold

principles.statement: Many systems can be split into simple patterns that each behave on their own, like the separate notes in a sound. Each pattern is described by a single number, such as a frequency or an energy. The list of those numbers then answers many questions about the whole system. The patterns themselves also serve as natural building blocks, so that anything else on the system can be described by how much of each pattern it contains.
principles.title: Breaking a system into independent modes turns it into a list of numbers

principles.statement: Move an arrow, a phase or a frame around a closed loop while keeping it as unchanged as the space allows. Around a small loop, any change on return measures the curvature inside the loop. Around a loop that encircles a region it cannot be shrunk through, a change can appear even where the space along the path is flat, and it then records what the loop encloses. Forces in physics can be read as this kind of curvature.
principles.title: Carrying something around a loop and finding it changed measures curvature

principles.statement: Suppose some members of a collection contain others, and any two members have a smallest member containing both and a largest member contained in both. These two operations then obey the same few rules whatever the members are. Extra rules, such as overlap distributing over joining, pick out narrower families, and each narrower family inherits what was proved for the wider one. The sub-parts of an algebraic structure and the divisors of a number are handled this way.
principles.title: Collections ordered by containment share one set of rules for joining and overlapping

principles.statement: The entropy that governs heat and disorder is defined by a formula of the same form as the uncertainty that information theory counts in bits, and it can be read as the information still needed to pin down a system's exact microscopic state. Physical law ties the two together: erasing a bit held in a physical memory gives off at least a fixed small amount of heat. Irreversibility can likewise be measured as an information distance between a process and the same process run backward.
principles.title: Entropy in heat measures missing information about a system's exact state

principles.statement: When some events must come before others but many pairs are unrelated, the constraints form a partial order. Such an order can always be extended to a single line that respects every constraint, which is how tasks are scheduled and how distributed systems agree on what happened first.
principles.title: Events that are only partly ordered can always be lined up consistently

principles.statement: Computing means moving charge, flux or heat, so physics sets the price. Erasing a bit has a minimum energy, signals take time to cross wires, and the behavior of devices as they shrink decides how fast and efficient chips can be.
principles.title: Every computation is a physical process with an energy and time cost

principles.statement: In small systems, quantities such as the work done or the entropy produced vary from one run to the next, and runs that go against the usual direction do occur. Exact relations fix how likely such runs are: compared with the usual runs they become exponentially rarer as the system or the observation time grows. The familiar one-way laws for averages, such as average work being at least the free-energy change, follow from these exact relations.
principles.title: Exact rules for rare fluctuations stand behind the one-way laws of averages

principles.statement: A hard choice among many options can be rewritten as an energy, where better answers have lower energy. Finding the best answer then means finding the lowest-energy state, which a physical system reaches only if it is cooled or changed slowly enough. Methods and insights move both ways: cooling schedules become search algorithms, and the physics of disordered materials explains when search gets hard.
principles.title: Finding the best answer is the same problem as a physical system settling into its lowest energy

principles.statement: In some settings the collection of all allowed functions from one object to another is itself an object of the same sort, and a function of two inputs is the same as a function that returns a function. Wherever this holds, programs that take and return functions can be given a meaning. The same structure appears in logic, in typed programming languages and in the ordered sets used to model computation.
principles.title: Functions between things of one kind can be treated as a thing of the same kind

principles.statement: Some features of a shape, such as how many holes it has or how many times something winds around, are whole numbers or other labels that come in separate steps. Such a label cannot change a little, so these features survive any small deformation or noise. Quantities that take exactly stepped values, and information protected by such features, are often explained this way.
principles.title: Global shape is recorded in whole numbers that small changes cannot alter

principles.statement: Measurements show effects, not the causes behind them. Working backward needs a model of how causes produce effects, a way to compare predictions with data, and a check of which causes the data can actually tell apart. The same backward reasoning serves astronomy, particle detectors, the Earth's interior and learning about quantum states.
principles.title: Hidden causes can be inferred from their measured effects

principles.statement: Data described by thousands of numbers often do not fill that whole space. Many real data sets appear to sit near a much smaller surface, and methods that find that surface, its shape and its natural coordinates can describe the data with far fewer numbers. This is a working assumption that many learning methods rely on, not a law.
principles.title: High-dimensional data often lie near a few hidden dimensions

principles.statement: Questions can be ranked by how many layers of 'there exists' and 'for all' are needed to state them, and that ranking tracks how much computing power is needed to answer them. Restricting to finite worlds, or to bounded resources, changes which logical tools still work.
principles.title: How hard a question is mirrors how complicated it is to state

principles.statement: Choosing one option out of many, or hitting one small target within a wide range, removes uncertainty, and the amount removed can be counted in bits: doubling the number of equally likely options adds one bit. Dividing that count by the time taken gives a rate, so people, devices and communication channels can be compared on the same scale. For human movement the count is an analogy with signalling and not a derived law.
principles.title: How hard it is to pick one target among many can be measured in bits

principles.statement: For a system in equilibrium, the size of its spontaneous random fluctuations and the size of its response to a small outside change are tied together. A system whose energy wanders widely by itself also takes up a lot of heat for each degree it is warmed. Measuring the jitter at rest therefore predicts the response to a push, and the reverse.
principles.title: How strongly a system responds to a push matches how much it jitters on its own

principles.statement: Say that a thing matters when the things pointing to it matter. This looks circular, but written as an equation it has, for a connected network, a single solution with no negative scores once the overall scale is fixed. That solution can usually be found by repeating the rule until the scores stop changing. Rankings of web pages, papers and people in networks are built this way.
principles.title: Importance can be defined in terms of itself and still have a definite answer

principles.statement: When many independent random events are combined, the result usually follows one of a few standard shapes, such as the bell curve or the law of rare events. Because those shapes are simple, quantities like noise levels, collision rates or correlations can be computed without knowing the details.
principles.title: Independent random events add up to a few universal distributions

principles.statement: Some calculations produce sums or integrals that come out infinite even though the measured answer is finite. Careful rules for setting the infinite part aside, applied the same way every time, recover the finite answer, and the rules themselves turn out to have a clean mathematical structure.
principles.title: Infinite sums can be given finite meaning by consistent rules

principles.statement: Whenever jobs arrive over time to use something that can serve only so much at once, the situation can be modelled as a waiting line. The model predicts how long jobs wait and how the order of service shifts that waiting between short and long jobs. Checkout counters, network routers and a computer's processor are all analysed this way.
principles.title: Jobs competing for a shared resource can be studied as a waiting line

principles.statement: Repeatedly blurring a system and asking how its description changes sorts its details into those that fade away and those that survive at large scales. The way a description flows under this zooming out is itself an object of study, and similar flows appear in geometry and possibly in layered learning systems.
principles.title: Looking at a system at coarser and coarser scales shows which details matter

principles.statement: Drop or soften some of a problem's requirements and the easier problem that remains can only do as well or better, so its best value bounds the true best value from one side. Such bounds are often cheap to compute and never mislead in the wrong direction. Search methods use them to rank options and skip ones that cannot win, and whole-number problems are bounded the same way by their fractional versions.
principles.title: Loosening the rules of a problem gives a safe estimate of its best answer

principles.statement: If some changes are declared not to matter, things that differ only by those changes can be lumped together. When the ignored changes fit well with the rest of the structure, the lumps combine by the same kind of rules as the originals. Setting aside a crystal's repeating shifts leaves the finite set of rotations and reflections used to classify crystals.
principles.title: Lumping together what differs only by an ignored change leaves a smaller structure of the same kind

principles.statement: When a job splits into many copies of the same small task that do not wait on one another, such as updating each particle, pixel or grid cell, many simple workers can do them all at once. How much faster this goes is limited by the parts that cannot be split and by the cost of moving data to the workers.
principles.title: Many copies of one small task can all be done at the same time

principles.statement: When very many parts each pull on all the others, following every pair is hopeless, but each part can often be treated as moving in the smooth average field that all the others make together. That field is itself computed from where the parts are, so the description has to be made consistent with itself. It works best when each part feels many others weakly, and it misses the effects of close encounters.
principles.title: Many interacting parts can be replaced by each one feeling the average of all the others

principles.statement: Fitting data, making predictions with uncertainty and simulating physics often end in a large system of linear equations. How fast and how reliably that system can be solved, by factoring it, by improving an approximate answer step by step, or by correcting the broad errors on a coarser version of the problem, decides what is practical.
principles.title: Many numerical problems come down to solving linear equations well

principles.statement: A path built from many tiny independent random steps spreads out in a predictable way. That spreading can be described exactly, and knowing how probability flows lets one reverse it: start from noise and steer back toward structured data, or treat noisy learning steps as a physical system near balance.
principles.title: Many small random kicks add up to diffusion which can be run backward

principles.statement: When people rank the options differently, some rule must turn their rankings into one group decision. With three or more options, no rule can meet a short list of fair-sounding requirements all at once, so choosing the rule is itself a decision. The same question arises whether the group is a set of voters or the people whose feedback shapes a trained system.
principles.title: Merging many people's preferences into one choice forces trade-offs

principles.statement: Two kinds of object may look unrelated yet combine by exactly the same rules. When that happens, every fact that follows from those rules alone holds for both. This is why a regular grid of points, a finite number system and a set of error-correcting codewords can all be handled with the familiar tools of arithmetic and linear algebra.
principles.title: Objects that look different can obey exactly the same rules of combination

principles.statement: Theories that differ in many details can still share one prediction. If a single precise enough measurement contradicts that shared prediction, every theory in the family fails at once, however different the rest of it is. Pinning down one number can clear away a large part of a field of rival explanations.
principles.title: One precise measurement can rule out a whole family of theories

principles.statement: In quantum theory the possible states of a system can be added and scaled like arrows. What we can observe, how states change in time, and the probabilities of measurement results are all read off from lengths, angles and projections in that space of arrows.
principles.title: Possible states form a space of vectors and probabilities come from its geometry

principles.statement: A proof can show that something must exist without saying how to find it. Some rules of reasoning, such as freely picking one member from every nonempty collection, give exactly such proofs, and a thing defined by them need not come with any way to compute it. Keeping track of which conclusions came with a recipe separates what can be built from what is only known to exist.
principles.title: Proving that something exists is not the same as being able to build it

principles.statement: Quantum systems can share correlations stronger than any classical mechanism allows. These correlations are treated as a resource, something costly to make that gets used up: they help with tasks in communication and computation, and they let two parties detect an eavesdropper on a secret key. Quantum computers, which draw on them, can also work out the energies of molecules in a time that grows far more slowly with size than on ordinary machines.
principles.title: Quantum correlations are a resource no classical system can supply

principles.statement: Points described by very many numbers can be squashed by a random mapping into a space with far fewer numbers while the distances between them change only by a small factor. How many numbers are needed depends on how many points there are and how small the change must be, not on how many numbers described each point at first. Any task that only needs distances, such as finding the closest match, can then be done in the smaller space.
principles.title: Random flattening into far fewer dimensions keeps distances nearly unchanged

principles.statement: Combining statements with and, or and not obeys the same rules as wiring switches in series and parallel, or taking overlaps and unions of sets. Any of these can be computed with the methods of the others, including ordinary algebra in which one plus one is zero.
principles.title: Reasoning with true and false follows the same algebra as switches and subsets

principles.statement: Start from nothing and apply a rule that only ever adds information, and that never gives less when it is given more. When the rule stops changing anything, the result is the smallest answer consistent with the rule. Database queries, program analysis, logic programs, replicated data and the meaning of recursive programs are all computed this way.
principles.title: Repeating a step that only adds information until nothing changes gives the smallest consistent answer

principles.statement: Many problems carry their own natural units of length, mass or time. Measured in those units, cases that differ only in overall size become the same problem, so one equation without units describes them all. Only the few numbers that cannot be scaled away still tell one case from another.
principles.title: Rescaling a problem by its own natural sizes can collapse many cases onto one curve

principles.statement: Methods that improve an answer a little at a time crawl when the problem is much steeper in some directions than in others, because a step that is safe in the steep directions barely moves along the shallow ones. Rescaling the problem so that all directions have similar steepness lets the same method take useful steps in every direction. A good rescaling must also be cheap to apply, and finding one is often the hard part.
principles.title: Rescaling a problem so every direction looks alike makes step-by-step methods fast

principles.statement: When a report is scored after the outcome is known, the scoring rule can be chosen so that the expected score is best for an honest report of what one actually believes. Exaggerating or hedging then loses on average. Such rules grade weather forecasters and train machines to say how sure they are, and the same design goal shapes auctions in which bidding what an item is really worth to you is the best move.
principles.title: Rewards can be arranged so that telling the truth is the best strategy

principles.statement: If every expression can be rewritten by fixed rules into a standard form, then deciding whether two expressions are equal becomes a mechanical comparison of their standard forms; when the form is unique, they are equal exactly when the forms match. For this to work the rewriting must always come to a stop and must end at the same place whichever rule is applied first. Arranging that is often the real work.
principles.title: Rewriting everything into one standard form settles whether two things are equal

principles.statement: Many laws are worked out for a system so large that its size no longer matters. In a small enough system, effects that the large-system picture averages away, such as the gaps between individual energy levels, become visible and the behavior changes. Comparing the small and the large case shows which features depend on size.
principles.title: Rules derived for very large systems change when the system is small

principles.statement: Data gathered under one set of conditions can stand in for data from different conditions. If one knows how much more or less likely each outcome is under the target conditions than under the ones that produced the data, weighting each sample by that ratio turns averages over the data into averages for the target. The weights become unreliable when the target puts weight where the data almost never fall.
principles.title: Samples from one distribution can answer questions about another once each is reweighted

principles.statement: When several agents each adjust to do better against the others, the only states where everyone stops adjusting are those where nobody gains by changing alone. Such states exist under mild conditions, but finding one can be hard and the adjusting need not settle at one. Simple learning rules do reach weaker forms of it.
principles.title: Self-interested agents adapting to each other can rest only where nobody gains by changing alone

principles.statement: If nothing but chance connects some labels or an ordering to the data, every rearrangement of them is as likely as the one observed. Comparing the real arrangement with many shuffled copies shows how often chance alone would give a result as extreme, without assuming a formula for the noise. A real arrangement that stands far out from its shuffles is evidence that something more than chance is at work.
principles.title: Shuffling the data shows what chance alone would produce

principles.statement: A small kit of simple building blocks, combined in enough ways, can approximate any reasonable target as closely as wanted. This is why networks of simple units can approximate arbitrary continuous functions and why a few basic operations suffice to approximate any quantum computation. It is also why such a network can be used as a stand-in for the unknown solution of an equation and trained to satisfy it.
principles.title: Simple pieces combined in enough ways can imitate any shape

principles.statement: A quantity can be found by repeatedly nudging a guess using measurements that are each unreliable. If the nudges shrink at a suitable rate, then for well-behaved problems the errors average out and the guess settles on the right value. Training a model one noisy step at a time is an instance of this older method.
principles.title: Small corrections from noisy measurements can still home in on the right answer

principles.statement: For many problems a proposed answer is quick to check but finding one seems to take enormous effort. That gap can be used: secrets can be protected by it, and proofs can convince without revealing anything beyond the truth of the claim. New kinds of computers could close the gap for particular problems.
principles.title: Some problems are easy to check but hard to solve and that hardness can be put to use

principles.statement: Build objects using only some basic operations and assume nothing extra, as when expressions are made from symbols or lists from adding one item at a time. Then any other setting that offers the same operations gives exactly one reading of those objects that respects the operations. Giving a program its meaning, adding up a list and evaluating a polynomial at a number all work this way. So does defining a function on such objects by saying what to do at each building step.
principles.title: Something built from its rules alone can be read in any setting that obeys those rules

principles.statement: Adding carefully structured extra symbols lets a receiver detect and repair errors, provided the noise is not too strong. The extra symbols keep valid messages far apart, so a slightly damaged message is still closest to the one that was sent. The structure is often built from arithmetic on a finite set of symbols, and the same idea protects fragile quantum information.
principles.title: Spreading information redundantly protects it from noise

principles.statement: Doing one step and then another is a kind of multiplication: it can be grouped either way, and doing nothing acts like the number one. Placing steps side by side is a second such multiplication. Machines that read symbols, patterns that describe text, and circuits of quantum gates can all be studied through this algebra of composition.
principles.title: Steps done one after another combine like multiplication

principles.statement: Among all the ways something could get from one place or state to another, the one that happens is the one that makes a total over the whole path as small as possible, or at least unchanged by small detours. The paths of light, of falling bodies and of planned decisions can all be found by solving such a best-path problem. The same kind of problem picks out the cheapest way to move one spread of mass into another, a route that a method can also adopt by design.
principles.title: The path actually taken makes a total cost as small as it can be

principles.statement: Asking for answers in whole numbers can make a best-choice problem much harder than allowing fractions. For some problems the constraints are arranged so that, when the given numbers are whole, a best fractional answer can always be found that is already whole. Then the easy method for the fractional problem solves the whole-number one too.
principles.title: The right structure makes a whole-number problem no harder than its fractional version

principles.statement: Anything written with finitely many symbols from a fixed alphabet belongs to a list that can be counted off one by one. Many collections, such as all endless strings of digits, are too large for any such list. So most of their members have no finite description at all, and no rule or program can produce them.
principles.title: There are far more possible things than finite descriptions of them

principles.statement: When items are sorted into groups inside groups, the distance between two items can be taken as the size of the smallest group containing both. Such distances obey a stronger rule than ordinary ones: of any three items, the two largest distances are equal. Numbers compared by how often a prime divides their difference, and the states of some disordered magnets, are organised this way.
principles.title: Things sorted into nested groups are as far apart as the smallest group that holds both

principles.statement: A good guess about what comes next lets a message be written in fewer symbols, and a short description is only possible when the data are predictable. Prediction error and compressed length can therefore be counted in the same units. No method can shorten every possible message, so every compressor bets on which messages are likely. When some loss is allowed, the task becomes keeping what matters in as few symbols as possible.
principles.title: To predict well is to compress well

principles.statement: When a system evolves, each point moves and carries quantities with it. Writing down how a carried quantity changes along the motion shows what the motion keeps fixed, such as the volume of a patch of possible states, and that is often the key to the whole dynamics. A step-by-step simulation built to keep the same things fixed tends to stay faithful to the true motion over long runs.
principles.title: Tracking what a flow carries along tells you what it preserves

principles.statement: Physics gives each possible state a weight that falls off with its energy. Many probabilistic models of data and belief use the same rule: write down a score for each configuration, turn it into a weight, and divide by the total. The tools for computing that total, and the trouble it causes, are shared.
principles.title: Uncertain beliefs are weighted the way energy weights states at a temperature

principles.statement: If a description must look the same after some change (a rotation, a relabelling, a shift in time, a change of measuring units), that requirement alone rules out most possible laws. What is left is organised by the ways the change can act. Conserved quantities, the classification of particles, the layers that a symmetry-respecting learning system may use, and the discarding of candidate formulas whose units do not match are all worked out by naming what must stay the same.
principles.title: What stays the same under a change of viewpoint fixes the form of the laws

principles.statement: When light, heat or a force spreads out evenly from a point and none of it is lost, the same total passes through every sphere around that point. Its strength at a given distance is the total divided by the area of that sphere. Because spheres grow faster in more dimensions, measuring how fast something weakens with distance tells how many directions it is spreading into.
principles.title: Whatever spreads evenly from a point thins out as the area it covers grows

principles.statement: Some problems have many answers that all fit the requirements perfectly. A search method that only cares about fitting will still end up at one particular answer, and which one depends on where it starts and how it moves. Knowing that hidden preference explains why the answer found often behaves better, or worse, than an arbitrary fitting answer would.
principles.title: When many answers fit equally well the way you search decides which one you get

principles.statement: If two kinds of object can meet and cancel, adding the same amount of both changes nothing that lasts. What survives is the difference between them. Counting such differences, the way negative numbers arise from comparing two counts, is how many algebraic invariants are defined. It is also how the charges of objects that can cancel against their opposites are proposed to be classified in string theory.
principles.title: When opposite things can cancel in pairs only their difference is conserved

principles.statement: If a known share of all candidates would do and each candidate is cheap to test, drawing candidates at random and testing them finds a good one after, on average, about as many tries as one divided by that share. Knowing how common good candidates are therefore turns a search with no formula into one with a predictable cost.
principles.title: When suitable answers are common enough guessing and checking finds one quickly

principles.statement: Counting arrangements depends on whether the things being arranged carry labels. Swapping two identical things gives nothing new, so there are fewer distinct arrangements than for labelled things. In physics, particles of the same kind cannot be told apart, and counting them this way changes which statistics they obey and how entropy is computed.
principles.title: Whether things can be told apart changes how many arrangements there are
